title: My palm is small
hook: Rumi: the eye of the senses is like a palm on the elephant, touching only part (Masnavi 3.1259ff)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the swarm: what isn't good for the hive isn't good for the bee. The hive.

Two people describe the same family dinner. One says it was lovely. The other says it was a disaster. They were at the same table. Two coworkers describe the same boss: one sees a tough mentor, the other a bully. Most arguments aren't between someone who's right and someone who's wrong. They're between people each holding a real piece of something too big to hold whole. Rumi told a story about that, one you may have heard in another form. In his version, it's very dark, and there's an elephant in the room.
screen: `SAME DINNER, TWO STORIES.` → `EACH HOLDING A REAL PIECE.` → `MY PALM IS SMALL.`

segments.voice: It's in Book Three of the Masnavi. Some travelers from India bring an elephant to a town where no one has ever seen one. They keep it in a dark house. Crowds come, but it's pitch black inside, so everyone has to feel it with their hands. One person's hand lands on the trunk. It's like a water pipe, he says. Another touches the ear: it's like a fan. Another finds a leg: no, it's a pillar. Another lays a hand on its back: it's like a throne. Each of them is describing something real. None of them is lying. And every one of them is wrong about the elephant. Then Rumi gives the key. The eye of the senses, he says, is only like the palm of the hand, and the palm can't reach all of the elephant. If each of them had carried a candle, their differences would have disappeared. The story is old. A version with blind men and an elephant appears much earlier in a Buddhist text called the Udana, and a Persian poet before Rumi, Sanai, told it too. Rumi's point is about how we know. Our senses, our opinions, our clever arguments are palms in the dark. They touch real things, but they're small, and the elephant is very large. So Rumi's candle isn't a better hand. It's a different kind of seeing, what Sufis call the eye of the heart. Before you insist it's a pillar, it's worth remembering where your hand is. Your line: remembering where your hand is.
screen: `AN ELEPHANT IN A DARK HOUSE.` · `A PIPE, A FAN, A PILLAR, A THRONE.` · `THE PALM CAN'T REACH IT ALL.` · then, large: `MY PALM IS SMALL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you're sure about, a person, a disagreement, a situation at home or work, and feel your hand on your piece of it. Then ask gently what someone at the other end might be touching, and what you'd see with a candle. You don't have to change your mind; just remember the size of the elephant.
Elephant. Rumi's image for a hidden whole: each hand in the dark touches something real, but none touches all of the elephant. Today's word.
Your line: remembering where your hand is. Every palm touches something real, and none holds it all. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 202 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE CALL IS THE ANSWER.`

howItsDone: The elephant story is told in several traditions; readers of Rumi usually take his version as a teaching on the limits of the senses and the need for the eye of the heart.

chat.says: In Rumi's elephant story, who was right about the elephant?
options: Each touched something real, but no one's palm could reach the whole elephant.
The one who touched the leg, since a pillar is closest to a whole elephant.
No one, because they were all lying to look clever in front of the crowd.
chat.meaning: Each hand touched something real, and none touched all of it. Rumi says the senses are like a palm in the dark; a candle would show the whole.

Masnavi.meaning: Rumi's long Persian poem of teaching stories, in six books

Udana.meaning: an early Buddhist text with a blind men and elephant story

Sanai.meaning: a Persian poet before Rumi who also told the story

Sufis.meaning: followers of the mystical path within Islam

Rumi.meaning: a 13th-century Persian Muslim poet and Sufi teacher

sources.ref: Masnavi 3.1259ff (the elephant in the dark house)
Udana 6.4 (the blind men and the elephant)
Sanai, Hadiqat al-Haqiqa (the elephant and the blind)
sources.work: Sanai, The Walled Garden of Truth (described)

notes: Paraphrased from Nicholson: the elephant brought by Hindus (rendered 'travelers from India'), the dark house, trunk/water-pipe, ear/fan, leg/pillar, back/throne, 'the eye of sense-perception is only like the palm of the hand', the candle. Confirm each.
Udana 6.4 and Sanai's Hadiqa as earlier versions: confirm references.

The story is often used to say all religions touch the same truth. The script deliberately keeps to Rumi's own point (the senses vs the eye of the heart) and avoids that reading, so as not to compare traditions.
